subject: Agriculture
title: The Rise of Monoculture
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Rise of Monoculture.

hook.text: Drive through Iowa and you'll see corn for miles—nothing else. This is monoculture.

buildup.text: Modern farming plants vast fields with a single crop. Machines harvest efficiently when every plant is identical.

discovery.text: Monoculture maximizes yield per acre. It's the cheapest way to produce grain at industrial scale.

twist.text: One disease can destroy an entire monoculture field. Genetic uniformity means shared vulnerability.

climax.text: The Irish Potato Famine killed a million people—caused by monoculture of a single potato variety.

punchline.text: All your eggs in one basket feeds millions—until it doesn't.

quiz.question: What is the main risk of monoculture farming?
options: A single disease can wipe out an entire crop due to genetic uniformity

details.summary: Monoculture—growing a single crop over large areas—became the dominant farming model in the 20th century. This topic explores how mechanization, chemicals, and markets drove monoculture expansion and why its ecological vulnerabilities are becoming harder to ignore.
details.whyItMatters: Monoculture maximizes short-term efficiency but depletes soil, breeds resistant pests, and leaves food systems dangerously dependent on a handful of crop species vulnerable to the same threats.
takeaways: Over 75% of US cropland grows just corn, soybeans, and wheat in rotations
Monoculture simplifies machinery use but increases vulnerability to pest epidemics
Genetic uniformity in monocultures makes entire harvests susceptible to a single disease

faq.question: Why did monoculture become the dominant farming system?
faq.answer: Mechanization favored uniform fields that machines could efficiently plant, spray, and harvest. Chemical inputs controlled the pest and disease problems monoculture creates, and commodity markets rewarded large volumes of standardized crops.

faq.question: What are the risks of monoculture farming?
faq.answer: Monoculture depletes specific soil nutrients, breeds resistant pests and diseases, reduces biodiversity, increases vulnerability to crop failure, and degrades soil health over time. The Irish Potato Famine is a historic example of monoculture risk.
